site.name: Columbia Mine
overview: The Columbia Mine was one of the best-known gold mines of the Ward Mining District, developed on the prominent Columbia vein near the top of Niwot Hill west of Ward.

Historic geological and archival sources identify the Columbia among the district's major producers and preserve photographs of its mine buildings, miners, and ore-handling activity from the late nineteenth to early twentieth century.

timeline.text: The Columbia vein was located during the first years of the Ward mining camp, helping establish the district's early hard-rock mining activity.
The Columbia became one of the Ward district's most important producing mines and was later associated with the Big Five mining properties.
Joseph B. Sturtevant photographed the Columbia Mine, preserving views of miners, mine buildings, and an ore cart at the property.

moreHistory: Historic geological reporting places the Niwot and Columbia mines near the top of Niwot Hill about half a mile west of Ward on the Columbia vein, a major vein system extending eastward across the district.

The same geological reporting describes the Niwot and Columbia as the greatest gold producers in the Ward district and states that much of the approximately $6 million in output later attributed to the Big Five properties came from these two mines before the Big Five Company was organized.
Carnegie Library for Local History catalog records identify the Columbia as one of the Big Five mines at Niwot Hill and preserve period photographs of miners and ore-handling activity at the site.

A USGS/GNIS-derived mapped mine point at approximately 40.03610, -105.53111 is used as a defensible mine-level identification point. Remnant does not represent this point as a field-surveyed surviving shaft or portal collar.
